# Adherence to the EAT-Lancet Planetary Health Diet and Cardiometabolic Risk Markers in the Mediators of Atherosclerosis in South Asians Living in America (MASALA) Study

**Authors:** Nilendra K Nair; Linh P Bui; Caleigh M Sawicki; Namratha R Kandula; Alka M Kanaya; Kyu Ha Lee; Meir J Stampfer; Walter C Willett; Shilpa N Bhupathiraju

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Nutrition, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston, MA, United States | 2Department of Global Health and Population, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston, MA, United States | 3Research Advancement Consortium in Health, Hanoi, Vietnam | 4Channing Division of Network Medicine, Brigham and Women’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, United States | 5Department of Epidemiology, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston, MA, United States | 6Division of General Internal Medicine and Geriatrics, Department of Medicine, Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine, Chicago, IL, United States | 7Division of General Internal Medicine, Department of Medicine, University of California, San Francisco, San Francisco, CA, United States | 8Department of Biostatistics, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston, MA, United States

## Abstract

The global food system significantly impacts environmental and human health, contributing to substantial greenhouse gas emissions.

We examined associations between a novel Planetary Health Diet Index (PHDI) that reflects adherence to the EAT-Lancet recommendations and cardiometabolic risk in a cohort of South Asians.

We analyzed data from MASALA study participants with baseline (n = 891) and 5-y follow-up (n = 735) data. The PHDI comprised 15 food components and ranged from 0 to a maximum of 140, with higher scores indicating greater adherence to the PHDI. We used multivariable linear and logistic regression models to examine cross-sectional and prospective (5-y) associations between baseline PHDI and cardiometabolic risk factors, adjusting for demographic, health, and lifestyle factors and baseline values of the outcome (prospective analyses only).

Among MASALA study participants (47% female, mean age 55 y), the mean PHDI score was 88.8 (SD 9.47). Prospectively, higher PHDI was associated with lower percentage difference in fasting glucose (−0.29 ± 0.15 %), glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) (−0.08 ± 0.04%), higher high-density lipoprotein (0.40 ± 0.17 mmol/L), lower body weight (−0.37 ± 0.12 kg), body mass index (BMI) (−0.08 ± 0.03 kg/m2), waist circumference (−0.49 ± 0.17 cm), and systolic blood pressure (−0.65 ± 0.30 mmHg) (P < 0.05 for all). Each 10-unit higher PHDI was associated with a 20% lower likelihood of incident type 2 diabetes (OR [95% CI]: 0.80 [0.54, 0.86]). Cross-sectionally, at baseline, 10 unit higher PHDI was associated with (β ± SE) lower percentage difference in fasting glucose (−0.45 ± 0.22 %) and HbA1c (−0.49 ± 0.22%), lower LDL (−0.015 ± 0.007 mmol/L), CRP (−5.40 ± 2.42 ug/L), higher adiponectin (4.67 ± 2.02 mg/dL), lower body weight (−0.59 ± 0.26 kg), BMI (−0.27 ± 0.11 kg/m2), waist circumference (−025 ± 0.29 cm), visceral fat (−1.37 ± 1.32 cm2), and pericardial fat (−0.58 ± 0.43 cm3) (P < 0.05 for all). Higher PHDI scores were associated with lower odds of obesity (OR [95% CI]: 0.80 [0.71, 0.92]) and overweight (0.77 [0.74, 0.85]).

Greater adherence to a planetary healthy diet was associated with lower cardiometabolic risk factors and risk of incident type 2 diabetes.

## Introduction

The modern global food system has a significant impact on both environmental and human health. It is responsible for 26% to 34% of the total global greenhouse gas emissions, with a majority coming from the agricultural sector, making it a major contributor to climate change [1]. With up to a third of global food production being wasted, the current food system is not operating in a sustainable manner, which in turn increases greenhouse gas emissions [2]. Furthermore, with 11 million premature deaths a year have been linked to unhealthy diets, the global food system has enormous negative effects on human health [[3], [4], [5]].

Cardiometabolic disorders, including coronary artery disease, stroke, and diabetes, are the leading causes of global morbidity and mortality; 3 of the top 10 global causes of death— coronary artery disease, stroke, and diabetes—account for more fatalities than the other top causes combined [6]. Studies suggest that South Asians in the United States, who account for 2% of the total United States population, have disproportionately higher rates of obesity and diabetes than other races and ethnic groups [[7], [8], [9]]. This is due to a combination of factors, including genetics (family history of disease), sociocultural factors [10], modifiable lifestyle [11,12], and dietary risk factors [13,14]. Although native South Asians share genetic and many cultural risk factors with the diaspora, South Asians in the United States differ in socioeconomic status, level of education, access to healthcare, and acculturation, which affect their risk [11,[15], [16], [17]]. Importantly, South Asian immigrants are adopting unfavorable dietary habits of their host countries, thereby replacing suboptimal South Asian dietary habits with potentially even more harmful Western dietary patterns [11,14,18,19].

In 2019, the EAT-Lancet Commission [20] released a Planetary Health diet that focuses on promoting the consumption of whole grains, fruits, vegetables, nuts, and legumes while limiting red and processed meats, added sugars, and refined grains. The Planetary Health diet is an evidence-based approach to dietary recommendations that could reduce the risks of chronic diseases and meet both human health and environmental goals. We have previously developed a Planetary Health Diet Index (PHDI) that quantifies the degree of adherence to the EAT-Lancet reference diet and demonstrated its validity in a South Asian population using data from the Mediators of Atherosclerosis in South Asians Living in America (MASALA) cohort [21]. Although the EAT-Lancet report was intended for the global food system, the health impacts of the EAT-Lancet diet across diverse populations are unclear, and its global adaptability has been subject to scrutiny.

The PHDI offers an evidence-based dietary approach to mitigate chronic disease risks while aligning with health and environmental objectives. Despite some studies indicating reduced risks of cardiovascular disease (CVD) [22] and type 2 diabetes (T2D) [23] with adherence to the EAT-Lancet diet, there is a paucity of data evaluating its potential effectiveness in individuals of South Asian descent. We, therefore, aimed to investigate the association between the PHDI and cardiometabolic risk factors in a cohort of United States South Asians.

## METHODS

### Study population

We used data from the MASALA study, a community-based prospective cohort of self-identified South Asians recruited from Chicago and the San Francisco Bay Area [24]. Eligibility criteria for the MASALA study included having South Asian ethnicity (≥3 grandparents born in any South Asian country), proficiency in English, Hindi, or Urdu, an age range of 40–84 y at baseline, and free of CVD at baseline. The baseline clinical examination took place from October 2010 to March 2013, enrolling a total of 906 participants. A follow-up examination was conducted 5 y later, between September 2015 and March 2018, with 749 participants returning for a follow-up assessment. Trained bilingual research staff collected data through questionnaires and secured written informed consent at the clinical field centers where participants were recruited [24,25]. All participants provided written formal study consent per their respective Institutional Review Boards (IRBs). The MASALA study protocol has been approved by the IRBs of University of California San Francisco and Northwestern University. The current analysis protocol has been approved by the IRB of Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Boston, Massachusetts.

### Dietary assessment and PHDI score

Dietary intakes over the past 12 mo were assessed using an ethnic-specific, validated, semiquantitative food frequency questionnaire (FFQ) [26]. The FFQ consists of 163 items, with 61 items unique to the South Asian diet. For each food item, the number of servings consumed per day was computed from the frequency (per day, week, month, year, or never) and the serving size (average, small, or large) as reported on the FFQ. The mean serving size was provided for each item, with a small serving equal to half the mean size and a large serving—1.5 times the mean. Detailed information on the nutrient profile of the FFQ food items has been previously documented in detail [24]. Participants with implausible energy intakes (defined as <800 kcal/d or >4000 kcal/d for men; <500 kcal/d or >3500 kcal/d for women) were excluded from the analysis.

The EAT-Lancet diet outlines 15 food groups with recommended consumption ranges for a 2500 kcal/d intake. Adaptation of the FFQ items into the 15 PHDI components has been previously detailed elsewhere [21]. Briefly, the FFQ's 163 food items were classified into 15 PHDI food groups, aligning with EAT-Lancet guidelines and South Asian dietary characteristics. We transformed serving sizes into grams using the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) Food Data Central database. Dishes unique to South Asian cuisine were disaggregated and converted to gram equivalents with the MyPyramid Equivalents Database 2.0 or the USDA Food Composition Database. The criteria for scoring the PHDI were previously developed and validated within the MASALA cohort (Supplemental Table 1). Scoring ranges for each of the 15 food groups align with the parameters defined by the EAT-Lancet reference diet [20]. The minimum score reflects the least positive impact of a food group on both health and the environment, whereas the maximum score indicates the highest level of favorable health and environmental effects associated with that food group. The thresholds for minimum and maximum scores vary based on whether the relationship between each food group and health outcomes is positive or negative. Intake between the minimum and maximum threshold was assigned proportionally. No deductions or additional scores are given for consumption falling outside the suggested range of the 15 food components. The total score ranged from 0 to 140.

### Cardiometabolic risk factors

#### Measure of glycemia and dyslipidemia

At baseline enrollment, several cardiometabolic risk factors were assessed, encompassing measures of glycemia, serum lipids, inflammation/adipokines, and body composition. These have been described in detail elsewhere [24]. Briefly, blood samples were collected following a 12-h fast. Fasting plasma glucose was determined using the hexokinase method (Ortho Clinical Diagnostics, Johnson & Johnson), and fasting insulin through a sandwich immunoassay (Roche Elesys 2010, Roche Diagnostics). Serum lipids consisting of total cholesterol, HDL cholesterol, and triglyceride were measured using enzymatic methods (Quest Diagnostics). LDL-cholesterol was calculated via the Friedwald formula. Insulin resistance was gauged using the HOMA-IR: fasting insulin(μIU/mL) × fasting glucose (mmol/L) ÷ 22.5 [27]. Insulin sensitivity was assessed using a surrogate measure of beta-cell function through the oral disposition index: ( Δ insulin0–30 ÷ Δ glucose0–30) × (1 ÷ fasting insulin) [28]. High sensitivity C-reactive protein was measured with the BNII nephelometer (Siemens Healthcare Diagnostics), and serum total adiponectin was ascertained via the Millipore Luminex adipokine panel A (EMD Millipore) [25].

#### Body composition measures

Standardized methods were employed for measuring weight, height, and waist circumference, with BMI calculated as [weight(kg)/height(m)2]. Asian-specific WHO cut-offs were applied to define overweight (BMI ≥23.0 kg/m2) and obesity (≥27.5 kg/m2) [24,29,30]. Abdominal visceral and subcutaneous fat areas were measured through computerized tomography (CT) scans of the abdomen, whereas noncontrast cardiac CT scans were used for pericardial fat volume and hepatic attenuation assessment (an inverse measure of hepatic steatosis). Fatty liver was defined by hepatic attenuation < 40 HU [24].

#### Subclinical atherosclerosis

High-resolution B-mode ultrasonography, employing the General Electric Vivid 7 ultrasound at the University of California, San Francisco, and the Siemens Acuson Sequoia C256 at Northwestern, was utilized for precise measurements of intima media thickness in the right and left internal and common carotid arteries [25]. The cardiac CT scans were conducted using either a Phillips 16D scanner or a Toshiba MSD Aquilion 64 at the University of California, San Francisco, and a Siemens Sensation Cardiac 64 Scanner at Northwestern, following established protocols [31]. Agatston scores were employed to assess coronary artery calcium in each of the 4 major coronary arteries, and the unadjusted sum of these scores was used for analysis [32].

#### Other cardiometabolic risk factors

Blood pressure was recorded as the average of 2 readings using an automated blood pressure machine (V100 Vital Signs Monitor, GE Healthcare). Hypertension was defined as blood pressure ≥140/90 mm Hg or the use of antihypertensive medication [25,33]. T2D was defined by the utilization of glucose-lowering medication, fasting plasma glucose concentrations ≥7.0 mmol/L, and/or glucose concentrations ≥11.1 mmol/L at 2 hours following a 75 g oral glucose challenge [24,33]. Incident diabetes and hypertension during the follow-up period were evaluated exclusively for participants who did not have T2D and hypertension at the baseline assessment.

#### Assessment of covariates

Participants provided written informed consent during visits to clinical field centers, where proficient bilingual research staff gathered information on various aspects. Covariates were chosen based on their established role as confounders in the diet-disease relationship within this cohort [15,33]. This included tobacco and alcohol usage, medical history, access to medical care, family history of CVD and T2D, and current use of prescription and nonprescription medications and supplements. Physical activity was evaluated using the Typical Week’s Physical Activity Questionnaire, quantified as total metabolic equivalent (MET) minutes per week [24]. Controlled hyperlipidemia was a composite variable defined as LDL-cholesterol within the target range based on cardiovascular disease risk level, determined by traditional risk factors such as age and family history of disease, the Framingham 10-y coronary artery disease risk score, and diabetes status. Additionally, a traditional cultural beliefs scale, comprising 7 items, was utilized to assess the sum of cultural traditional measures, with Likert scale scoring reflecting the strength of traditional South Asian beliefs (lower scores indicating stronger traditional beliefs) [15,24].

### Statistical analysis

The baseline characteristics of study participants across quartiles of the PHDI were compared. Statistical differences were assessed using linear regression and logistic regression models, adjusted for age, sex, and total energy intake for continuous variables, and the chi-square test for categorical variables. Linear trend tests were performed by assigning the median value to each quartile and treating it as a continuous variable in the regression model. Multivariable linear regression models were employed to assess the associations between the PHDI score (as a continuous exposure variable) and cardiometabolic risk factors. Assumptions of normality, linearity, and homogeneity were tested through examinations of residuals compared with predicted values and normal probability plots of residuals in all linear regression models. Outliers were identified through visual inspection of residual plots. In the presence of heteroscedasticity, outcome variables were log-transformed, and the residual plots were re-examined. Both continuous and dichotomized outcomes were included to provide a comprehensive perspective, with dichotomized measures facilitating clinical interpretation by aligning with established risk thresholds.

Four multivariable models were examined, with covariates added incrementally in a forward stepwise fashion. In the initial model, adjustments were made for age, sex, study site, education, smoking status, alcohol use, family history of diabetes, years lived in the United States, physical activity, the sum of cultural traditional measures, refined grain consumption, and total energy. As the PHDI does not include refined grains as a component, we decided to adjust for this variable in our analysis due to both its consumption in the cohort [19] as well as its association with increased cardiometabolic risk among individuals of South Asian descent [34]. In model 2, we further adjusted for diabetes medication use, cholesterol-lowering medication use, and hypertension medication use. Because BMI and waist circumference are potential mediators of the relationship between diet and cardiometabolic risk factors [23,33], we also adjusted for BMI in model 3 with an additional adjustment for waist circumference in model 4. All reported results are based on model 4.

For all prospective associations, adjustments included baseline values of covariates and the corresponding outcome measure. To minimize confounding due to prevalent disease, participants with T2D were excluded from follow-up glycemia measures. Linear association results are presented as the unit change in the outcome per 10-unit higher PHDI score. Potential effect modifications by age and sex were explored by including a cross-product term between these variables and the PHDI score in the model. Given the exploratory nature of interaction analyses and the increased risk of false positives, a more conservative threshold (P < 0.001) was used for statistical significance, a standard approach in epidemiologic studies for post-hoc analyses [33]. Main effects were evaluated at P < 0.05 as they were prespecified hypotheses. To assess potential selection bias in the prospective analysis, we compared baseline characteristics of participants who completed follow-up with those who did not (Supplemental Table 2). All tests were 2-sided and conducted using SAS, version 9.4, and in R 4.2.3.

## RESULTS

### Baseline characteristics

At baseline, 47% of the participants were female, with an average age of 55 y and BMI of 25.5 ± 3.9 kg/m2. The average PHDI scores ranged from 77.8 ± 0.4 (mean ± SEM) to 102.3 ± 0.3 in the lowest compared with highest quartile. Participants in the highest quartile compared with the lowest quartile of PHDI scores had lived in the United States for slightly fewer years, held stronger traditional cultural beliefs, were less likely to be current or former smokers, had higher family income, and were more likely to have a bachelor's degree or higher educational attainment (Table 1). No significant differences were observed in terms of country of birth, physical activity, weight, BMI, or waist circumference. ### Prospective analysis

In prospective analyses conducted ∼5 y after the baseline visit, each 10-unit higher PHDI score was associated with lower percentage difference in fasting glucose (−0.29 ± 0.15%; P = 0.05) and HbA1c in the fully adjusted model (−0.08 ± 0.04%; P = 0.03) (Table 2). Likewise, higher PHDI scores were associated with higher HDL cholesterol (0.40 ± 0.17 mmol/L; P = 0.02) but not triglycerides or LDL-cholesterol. Follow-up assessments of body composition revealed that a 10-unit higher PHDI score was associated with lower body weight (−0.37 ± 0.12 kg; P = 0.003), BMI (−0.08 ± 0.03 kg/m2; P < 0.03), and waist circumference (−0.49 ± 0.17 cm; P = 0.005). Associations between the PHDI score and odds of incident disease are depicted in Figure 1. Each 10-unit higher PHDI was associated with 20% lower odds of incident diabetes (odds ratio [OR]: 0.80; 95% CI: 0.54, 0.86). Although not statistically significant, in the fully adjusted model, each 10-unit higher PHDI score was associated with a 9% lower odds of incident hypertension (OR: 0.90; 95% CI: 0.66, 1.04). We did not observe any indications of effect modification by age or sex in the associations between the PHDI and cardiometabolic risk markers (P-interactions > 0.001). Attrition analysis (Supplemental Table 2) showed that participants lost to follow-up watched more TV per week (646.8 compared with 525.3 minutes, P = 0.007), had a slightly higher BMI (26.5 compared with 25.8 kg/m2, P = 0.05), and higher systolic blood pressure (127.7 compared with 123.9 mm Hg, P = 0.005) compared with those who returned for the follow-up visit. ### Cross-sectional analysis

Table 3 presents cross-sectional associations between the PHDI and cardiometabolic risk measures. Among participants without T2D at baseline, each 10-unit higher PHDI score, after multivariable adjustment for BMI and waist circumference, was associated with (β ± SE) lower fasting glucose (−0.45 ± 0.21 mmol/L; P = 0.03) and HbA1c (−0.5 ± 0.22%; P = 0.04). We found no association between PHDI and beta-cell function. On the other hand, although higher PHDI scores were associated with lower insulin resistance, this association did not reach statistical significance. Higher PHDI scores were associated with favorable measures of body composition and ectopic fat measures. For example, a 10-unit higher PHDI score was associated with a 0.59 kg lower body weight (P = 0.02), a 0.27 kg/m2 lower BMI (P = 0.01), and a 0.25 cm lower waist circumference (P = 0.03). Similarly, following BMI adjustment, a higher PHDI score was associated with a smaller visceral fat area (−1.37 ± 0.69 cm2; P = 0.04) and a smaller pericardial fat volume, which remained significant after additional adjustment for waist circumference (−0.58 ± 0.29 cm3; P = 0.05). We found no evidence of an association between PHDI score and subclinical measures of atherosclerosis.

Cross-sectional associations between PHDI scores and odds of disease are presented in Figure 1. In multivariable-adjusted models, for each 10-unit higher PHDI score, there were 20% lower odds of obesity (OR: 0.80; 95% CI: 0.71, 0.92) and a 23% lower likelihood of overweight (OR: 0.77; 95% CI: 0.74, 0.85). Although nonsignificant, after adjusting for BMI and waist circumference, each 10-unit higher PHDI was associated with a 15% lower likelihood of metabolic syndrome (OR: 0.85; 95% CI: 0.69, 1.06). No significant associations were identified with hypertension or fatty liver disease.

## Discussion

In this study involving a prospective cohort of South Asian adults in the United States, we found that greater adherence to the EAT-Lancet Planetary Health Diet, assessed by the PHDI, was associated with a favorable cardiometabolic risk profile. In cross-sectional analysis, stronger adherence to the PHDI was beneficially associated with outcomes in glycemic control, blood lipids, inflammatory markers, and adiposity measures. In prospective analysis, higher adherence to the PHDI was additionally associated with a lower risk of incident T2D. These associations persisted after adjusting for various known confounders in this population. To our knowledge, the current study is the first to investigate and generate evidence in a South Asian population on the association between adherence to the EAT-Lancet dietary guidelines and incident T2D. Our findings suggest that a diet aligning with the planetary healthy diet may serve as an effective strategy to prevent cardiometabolic risk in a high-risk South Asian population while potentially concurrently addressing the impact of global food systems on the climate crisis.

Excess adiposity, encompassing both visceral and ectopic fat, is linked to heightened cardiometabolic risk factors, including insulin resistance, chronic inflammation, dyslipidemia, and hypertension [35]. This elevated risk contributes to an increased susceptibility to cardiometabolic diseases. Previous evaluations of adherence to the EAT-Lancet diet using various scoring methods have yielded results consistent with our findings regarding its influence on cardiometabolic risk profile. In a prospective cohort of 59,849 adults from the United Kingdom (UK) Biobank, the authors discerned that 40% of the association of the EAT-Lancet diet pattern score with T2D could be ascribed to waist circumference, whereas 44% of the association was attributable to BMI [23]. Similarly, in the prospective NutriSante cohort of 62,382 participants, the association between the EAT-Lancet diet and cardiovascular disease was largely mediated by BMI [36]. In addition, in the ELSA-Brasil cross-sectional study of 14,515 Brazilian adults, higher EAT-Lancet diet scores were associated with an inverse relationship with indicators of obesity, including lower LDL-cholesterol, systolic blood pressure and non-HDL cholesterol [37]. High adherence to the EAT-Lancet diet was associated with lower BMI and waist circumference, with a 24% lower likelihood of being overweight or obese [37]. Moreover, these individuals were also 27% less likely to have a substantial increase in waist circumference compared with those with lower adherence. However, differences in scoring methods may influence findings. Although our approach aligns with established dietary indices (e.g., HEI, AHEI, PHD) used in large cohort studies, future studies could explore how associations compare across alternative EAT-Lancet scoring methods. Consistent with prior research, our findings demonstrated strong associations with BMI and obesity, suggesting that adherence to the PHDI is associated with healthier body weight and composition. The attenuation of other risk associations after adjusting for BMI and waist circumference suggests that a substantial part of the observed associations between PHDI adherence and other cardiometabolic risk outcomes is mediated through its impact on body weight and central adiposity.

Prior research focusing on assessing adherence to the EAT-Lancet diet, using binary scoring mechanisms, and its relationship with T2D have reported results consistent with our study. In the prospective Mexican Teachers’ Cohort, López et al. [38] observed a protective association with a 10% lower risk of T2D for those with higher adherence to the EAT-Lancet healthy reference diet score. Similarly, in the Danish diet, Cancer and Health cohort study, stronger adherence to the EAT-Lancet dietary guidelines was associated with a 19% decreased risk of T2D onset, indicating potential public health benefits [39]. The European Prospective Investigation into Cancer and Nutrition-Oxford study also demonstrated favorable associations between high adherence to the EAT-Lancet reference diet and diabetes risk [22], and a prospective cohort of 59,849 adults from the UK Biobank without prior diabetes diagnoses demonstrated that each incremental point increase in the diet score correlated with a 6% decrease in the risk of T2D [23]. More recently, Zhang et al. [40] examined the relationship between the EAT-Lancet diet T2D in 24,494 adults from the Malmö Diet and Cancer study. In contrast to the binary scoring mechanisms, the authors implemented a gradual scoring system akin to the approach used in our investigations. The Malmö Diet and Cancer cohort findings revealed a dose-response relationship across percentiles, with the highest adherence to their EAT-Lancet diet index being associated with an 18% decreased risk of T2D. Notably, this association remained robust after accounting for participants’ genetic predisposition to T2D and through multiple sensitivity analyses. Intriguingly, in our study, we note potential reverse causation in the relationship between chronic disease and diet quality such that participants in the highest quartile compared with the lowest quartile of PHDI scores were diagnosed with diabetes, hypertension, or hypercholesterolemia. This reverse causation has been previously observed in the CARRS study on South Asians [41], wherein South Asian adults in urban areas were adopting healthier dietary choices postdiagnosis [42,43]. Because PHDI was assessed only at baseline, we were unable to capture dietary changes over time, which may have attenuated the observed associations. Future studies with repeated dietary assessments can better account for these changes and clarify the directionality of these relationships.

Various potential mechanisms may underlie the observed favorable associations of the PHDI with cardiometabolic risk markers and T2D. The plant-based, nutrient-dense foods emphasized by the EAT-Lancet diet are rich in dietary fiber, antioxidants, unsaturated fats, and micronutrients, which support improved glycemic control, enhanced insulin sensitivity, decreased chronic inflammation, and improved weight control [44,45]. Additionally, the de-emphasis on food associated with heightened cardiometabolic risk, such as red and processed meats, saturated fats, and added sugar, strengthens the ameliorative advantages. A prior MASALA study investigating plant-based indices demonstrated similar findings regarding the impact of a healthy plant-based diet on cardiometabolic outcomes, in contrast to an unhealthy plant-based diet [33]. Although we did not make the distinction, it is worth noting that the quality of a plant-based diet and the extent of processing may play a crucial role in the observed associations [33]. The exclusion of refined grains from the PHDI could also impact certain metabolic markers, potentially explaining the nonsignificant prospective associations noted with triglycerides and LDL-cholesterol. This aligns with findings from Radhika et al. [34] in the Chennai Urban Rural Epidemiology Study, in which high consumption of refined grains in an Indian cohort was associated with higher waist circumference, serum triglyceride, and LDL-cholesterol.

Our study has notable strengths, including a prospective cohort comprising individuals of South Asian heritage with extensive data on cardiometabolic risk and measures of subclinical atherosclerosis. The comprehensive design of the MASALA study allowed consideration and control for confounding due to ethnic-specific measures beyond the traditional risk factors. Additionally, employing a validated South Asian-specific FFQ for dietary data enabled the development of the PHDI that incorporated culturally significant foods widely consumed within the South Asian diaspora. This allowed our approach to align with the design intent of the 2019 EAT-Lancet report, enabling local interpretation that reflects the culture and demography of the population. Moreover, to our knowledge, this is the first investigation that highlights the ameliorative benefits of the PHDI on cardiometabolic risk markers and diseases in a South Asian population, thereby providing further evidence to the ongoing discourse for the need to promote healthy and sustainable diets in South Asian countries. Nevertheless, it is important to interpret our results within the context of certain limitations. First, as with most observational studies, although we adjusted for a large number of known confounders in this population, we cannot entirely rule out the possibility of residual or unmeasured confounding. Our study did not adjust for multiple comparisons as our analyses focused on prespecified, complementary cardiometabolic risk markers that collectively assessed the impact of PHDI adherence on cardiometabolic health. Similar to prior MASALA studies [33], our outcomes, such as glycemic control, inflammatory markers, and adiposity, are biologically linked, providing a coherent and clinically relevant interpretation of diet-disease relationships while attempting to minimize type II error. Complete data on all cardiometabolic risk factors were not available for the prospective analysis. The limited number of incident diabetes cases constrained our power for prospective analysis. Additionally, we were not able to investigate environmental outcomes in the present study. However, our previous investigation has demonstrated the positive impact of the PHDI in the MASALA cohort on lower greenhouse gas emissions and dietary carbon footprint [21]. Finally, although our findings provide valuable insights, the generalizability may be limited by the cohort’s demographic composition. The study population primarily consists of middle-aged to older-aged South Asian individuals with higher income and education levels, which may not reflect the broader South Asian diaspora or populations with greater socioeconomic diversity. Although we adjusted for these factors in our models, we did not investigate income or education as effect modifiers due to the limited variability within our cohort, reducing statistical power to detect interactions. Future research in more socioeconomically diverse populations is needed to assess whether socioeconomic disparities influence adherence to Planetary Health diets and their associated cardiometabolic benefits.

In conclusion, our findings provide the first prospective evidence indicating that adherence to the PHDI is associated with a lower risk of incident T2D and favorable cardiometabolic risk measures in a South Asian population. Given the EAT-Lancet diet's inherent design to benefit both human and Planetary Health, our findings support the notion that adopting a diet aligned with 2019 EAT-Lancet recommendations may contribute to preventing T2D and improving cardiometabolic risk in a high-risk population, concurrently addressing the environmental impact of the food system on anthropogenic climate change.
